_what_this_is: What follows when a capability in the grant meets an asset in the deployment. Each is explicit, second person, in the mailbox's own words. `requires` names the capabilities, assets and other consequences it needs; `kind` is read | act | exfiltrate | disrupt | impersonate | outlive; `route` is the door out for an exfiltration; `evidence` is a tier from the vocabulary with a source and a date; `links` name nodes in data/standards/ by id; `questions` are what is not known, kept here rather than in a footnote. The barrier on a consequence is derived by the build from its required capabilities and is not typed here. No consequence carries a severity, a likelihood or a score. This site's extension of abp.sgit.ai v0.3.0, declared as such.
authored_by: the site, from the grant and the vendors' own pages; written to be argued with

consequences.statement: You can read any secret that has ever arrived in this mailbox: a password sent in plain text, an API key, an invitation.
consequences.source: read.message.tenant is measured; that secrets are among the messages is inferred — no scope separates them
questions: None on the reach itself; the open question is asset.secrets-in-mail, which the deployer can untick if this mailbox holds none.

consequences.statement: You can read every password-reset link and one-time code in this mailbox, past and future, for whatever other accounts use this address.
consequences.source: the same reading capability; reset mail and one-time codes are messages

consequences.statement: Because this deployment can also open a link, you can take over any account that resets its password by email to this address: read the reset link, follow it, set a new password.
consequences.source: the third leg — opening the link — is not the Gmail connector; it is Claude's own web fetch, which the project lead confirmed is on in this deployment (2026-09-16). The connector reads the mail; web fetch follows the link. Take away either and the takeover is gone.
questions: Whether the reset flow of a given service completes from a link alone, or asks for a second factor the mailbox does not hold, is per-service and not settled here.

consequences.statement: You can send any message in this mailbox to anyone — messages the sender authorised the account holder to read, not to forward.
consequences.route: a reply, a forward, or a new message carrying the content, sent as the account holder
consequences.source: read is measured; send is measured (one message, 2026-09-16); the asymmetry between reading and forwarding is a matter of authorisation and is recorded here as a claim about rights, not a legal finding
questions: Where the mailbox is a corporate one, the employer's own policy governs forwarding. This vault records that rights are held by the senders and the employer; it does not rule on whether a given forward is lawful.

consequences.statement: You can collect every address and every message body the mailbox holds, and assemble them.
You can send messages at whatever rate the platform allows, to as many recipients as it allows, as the account holder.
consequences.source: send is measured for one message; the rate and recipient limits, and what a burst triggers, are Google's and are documented from Google's pages or left open — never provoked on a live account
questions: Gmail's per-account sending limits, and whether the connector's send is subject to them, are not yet read from Google's pages. See RESEARCH-NEEDED.md.

consequences.statement: You can send payloads, links and pretexts to other people and other organisations, from a real account they may trust.
consequences.source: follows from send; internal recipients are the most exposed, because a message from a colleague's real address clears the filters a stranger's would not

consequences.statement: Sending enough, fast enough, may have Google suspend the account, and on a Workspace domain possibly the organisation.
consequences.source: Google operates sending limits and abuse protections; the sequence that suspends an account, and one that reaches the organisation, is read from Google's pages and dated, never triggered to find out
questions: The exact thresholds and the sequence of events are not yet read from Google's pages. Documented only; never measured.

consequences.statement: You can relabel, archive, trash or mark every message, undoing the filing the account holder built to find things.
consequences.source: the gmail.modify scope on the consent screen reads "Read, compose, and send emails from your Gmail account" and permits changing labels and moving messages; which of these the connector's tools expose is a research row. Permanent deletion is out of reach — the widest consented scope is gmail.modify, which does not bypass Trash.
questions: Whether the connector exposes tools to change a message's labels, archive, trash, mark read or mark spam — and whether any of these can be done in bulk — is not settled from either vendor's page. Two of these (change one label, mark one read) may be checked on the deployer's own account without provoking anything; the bulk versions are documented, never run.

consequences.statement: You can create a filter that forwards future mail to an outside address, with nobody present — exfiltration that outlives the session.
consequences.route: a Gmail filter with a forward action, running on every future message after the chat ends
consequences.source: a filter is the create.schedule.tenant row; whether create_filter runs under the three consented scopes, and whether a filter it makes can forward to an outside address, is a research row
questions: Does create_filter work under the consented scopes, and can its filter forward to an outside address? See RESEARCH-NEEDED.md.

consequences.statement: Mail you send carries nothing on its face that identifies it as sent by an agent rather than by the account holder.
consequences.source: measured 2026-09-16: the sent message's headers carry only a Received line from gmailapi.google.com with a numeric project id; no header names Claude or the connector as the author
questions: Whether the numeric sender in the Received line can be tied back to the connector's OAuth client, and whether any published method lets a recipient tell an agent-sent message from a person-sent one, is a research row.

provenance.note: Authored on this site from the grant, the deployer's measured run and the vendors' own pages. Every consequence is a claim about this deployment shape, none about Google or Anthropic as a party. Where a consequence is documented rather than measured, it was read from a page and never provoked on a live account.
